newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE-Austria's Red Bull rages into energy drink ring.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Austria's Red Bull rages into energy drink ring.

text.p: Austria's Red Bull has led a stampede into the fast-growing energy drinks arena, taking 90 percent of the domestic market and a 30 percent share in Europe, and its success shows no signs of fizzling out.
With twice the caffeine of coke, Red Bull is a hit among Europe's clubbers, many of whom have taken to mixing it with vodka to give them pep on the dance floor.

Red Bull sold 50 million cans last year in Austria in a population of eight million, compared with 150 million cans worldwide. The company expects to beef up its sales by some 25 percent this year in Europe, where it is sold in 20 countries.

"We see growth of 20 to 25 percent in Europe this year and accelerated growth to the year 2000 because we are in our first or second marketing year in about 14 countries, which means turnover will explode yearly," marketing director Norbert Kraihammer told Reuters in an interview at the company headquarters in Fuschl, near Salzburg.

At a retail price of 16 schillings ($1.34) per can, the company's turnover in 1997 could be expected to be around three billion schillings, although Kraihammer declined to make any forecasts or give last year's figures.
Consultancy group Zenith International predicts the energy drink sector will be one of the strongest growing markets in Europe in the next three years.
"My view is there's a lot more life in the energy concept across Europe," chairman Richard Hall said.
At the last count Zenith gave the European energy drink market a retail value of nearly $500 million, the equivalent of 75 million litres in 1995, up 82 percent on the year before.
Hall predicts consumption will more than double by the year 2000 to 200 million litres.
RED BULL LEADS PACK OF ENERGY DRINKS
Red Bull was launched in 1987 and rapidly became a hit in Austria, which has the highest per capita consumption of energy drinks in Europe at 2.8 litres per head in 1995.
In Germany and Switzerland too, night-clubbers dance the night away with the aid of Red Bull, paying up to three times the price of a can of Coke for the sweet yellowish liquid.
"The reason the market is of interest is that young people are working hard and playing hard and this is a socially acceptable way of gaining energy," Zenith's Hall said.
But Red Bull says the brands which specifically target the club-going MTV generation are on the wrong track.

"For us the biggest failure of our competitors is to target the clubbing scene, which is limiting and extremely misleading in the understanding of the product," said Kraihammer, a key figure in an informal team who prefer casual wear to suits.

The key to its success, Red Bull says, lies in the ingredients, which combine hefty doses of amino-acid taurine, vitamin B and caffeine to give a powerful injection of energy to grannies, students and sports players alike.
The company has recently started supplying old people's homes in Austria, Kraihammer said.

Its success has spawned over 30 brands in Austria alone, with names like Dark Dog, Blue Sow and Power Horse, but many of these have been forced to turn their attention abroad, dwarfed by the strength of Red Bull in their homeland.
"We are a mosquito to Red Bull's elephant," said Dark Dog trading head Siegfried Distl. They sold two million cans in Austria in 1995 and aim for sales of three million in 1997.
RED BULL FACES OBSTACLES OVER CONTENT
France and Italy refuse to allow Red Bull to be sold, citing health concerns.

The company also got into legal difficulties with advertising bodies in Britain over its claim that Red Bull revitalised the body and had to change its advertising strategy to call the product a stimulation rather than energy drink.
The cans carry the warning: "Caution: do not drink when you want to sleep".
Kraihammer dismisses worries about the high caffeine content of Red Bull as political rather than scientific.
The can contains the same amount of caffeine as a cup of medium filter coffee, equivalent to 320 mg per litre, he notes. Coca Cola contains 125 mg of caffeine per litre.
"I see it in the same way as functional food. You drink it when you need it. It's not a thirst quencher and you don't drink it for taste," Kraihammer said.
Red Bull spends around $60 million on marketing the slim blue and silver can through animated television and cinema advertisements and Formula One motor-racing sponsorship.
The core target group is aged from 14 to 40.
The company claims the drink improves reaction time and concentration, but emphasises it is not an isotonic, which replenishes lost minerals.
RED BULL LOOKS TO U.S. MARKET
Red Bull says as well as developing its European markets it aims to turn its attention to the United States, where it was approved two months ago.
"I think there is huge potential in the United States because we are so different to what is available there," Kraihammer said.
The firm is already testing a second product on the Austrian market but would not give any details.
The small company of around 100 employees has no plans to go public.
"We have the privilege of irrational decision without interference and that makes us extremely fast and flexible," Kraihammer said.
